abstract: |
  This article presents scaling (JS) and aggregated (JSA) James–Stein
  estimation of structural equation models, based on their implementation in
  the R package lavaan. Starting from a worked example, we describe the
  estimation of factor loadings and latent regression slopes equation by
  equation, followed by the estimation of variance, covariance, and intercept
  parameters. We also provide analytical standard errors for JS and JSA using
  the delta method, accounting for uncertainty across all estimation stages.
  Throughout, model-implied instrumental-variable (MIIV) estimation serves as
  a point of comparison within a common notation. A simulation study compares
  the standard error accuracy of JS and JSA with that of MIIV and maximum
  likelihood (ML) under correct model specification. The standard errors of
  JS and JSA perform comparably to those of MIIV and ML under the conditions
  examined.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(lavaan)
library(simhelpers)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
```

Structural equation models (SEMs) with latent variables are usually estimated
by maximum likelihood (ML), which estimates all parameters jointly. Although
ML has desirable asymptotic properties when its assumptions hold
[@browne_1984], difficulties can arise when it is applied in practice. For instance, a 
misspecification in one equation can
bias estimates in other equations [@kaplan_1988; @bollen_etall_2007;
@bollen_2018; @dhaene_rosseel_2023; see also @jin_etall_2021, for diagonally
weighted least squares], and the iterative optimization can fail to converge
or end in inadmissible solutions, especially in small samples [@bollen_2018;
@dhaene_rosseel_2023]. Equation-by-equation estimators offer an alternative
[e.g., @bollen_1996; @burghgraeve_etall_2021]. With these approaches,
factor loadings and latent regression slopes are estimated one equation at a
time and in closed form, which may limit the propagation of misspecification
across equations [@bollen_gates_fisher_2018; @burghgraeve_etall_2021] and
avoids iterative optimization for this part of the estimation.

This article focuses on James–Stein estimation, an equation-by-equation
estimator proposed for SEMs with latent variables in
@burghgraeve_etall_2021, which replaces each latent predictor by an estimate
of its conditional expectation given observed proxies and then applies
least squares. This conditional expectation is estimated using
James–Stein type shrinkage [@james_stein_1961; @efron_morris_1973;
@efron_morris_1975], and the approach follows the principle of regression
calibration in errors-in-variables regression [@fuller_1987;
@whittemore_1989; @carroll_etall_2006]. James–Stein estimation comes in a
scaling version (JS), which uses the scaling indicators as proxies, and an
aggregated version (JSA), which uses reliability weighted sums of
indicators. JSA was found to outperform ML and
model-implied instrumental-variable (MIIV) estimation in terms of mean
squared error under the small sample conditions examined
[@burghgraeve_etall_2021], and both versions were further evaluated for
confirmatory factor models by @dhaene_rosseel_2024. Moreover, throughout this 
article, we also use MIIV estimation as a point of comparison. MIIV is one of
the more widely known equation-by-equation estimators for SEMs and also
replaces each latent variable by a scaling indicator, but corrects for the
resulting measurement error with instruments implied by the model rather
than with an estimated reliability adjustment [@bollen_1996;
@bollen_bauer_2004; @bollen_2018]. Placing the two side by side makes clear what James–Stein 
estimation shares with MIIV and where it departs from it.

Beyond point estimation, the usefulness of James–Stein estimation for
statistical inference depends on the accuracy of its standard errors.
@burghgraeve_etall_2021 derived a sampling variance expression for latent
regression estimates that accounts for uncertainty in the estimated
reliability adjustment, providing a basis for analytical standard errors for
those estimates. However, they did not develop a complete analytical
standard error calculation for all model parameters and used bootstrap
standard errors for both JS and JSA in their empirical evaluations. For
MIIV, by contrast, standard errors are well established. Conventional
standard errors for factor loadings and latent regression slopes follow from
two-stage least squares [@bollen_1996]. Standard errors for these same
estimates can also be obtained by the delta method, using derivatives with
respect to the sample moments, for which @fisher_bollen_2020 provided
explicit analytical expressions. These derivatives also propagate
uncertainty in the estimated loadings and slopes into the standard errors of
subsequently estimated variance and covariance parameters. Standard errors
for these latter parameters were derived under unweighted least squares by
@bollen_maydeuolivares_2007 and extended to general weight matrices by
@jin_etall_2021. More recently, @maydeuolivares_etall_2026 compared
subsequent variance and covariance estimation procedures and the accuracy of
their standard errors. The R package lavaan [@rosseel_2012] now provides
analytical standard errors for JS and JSA by applying the delta method to
the complete estimation procedure. In addition, its JS and JSA
implementations, initially restricted to confirmatory factor models, have
been extended to more general models, and the package also includes MIIV
estimation.

## Present Study and Contributions

This article makes three minor contributions. First, it describes
James–Stein estimation, as implemented in lavaan, and conceptually compares
it with MIIV estimation within a common notation, starting from a worked
example in which the two estimators are applied to the same equation.
Second, it develops and
illustrates a complete delta method calculation of standard errors for JS
and JSA, accounting for uncertainty
across all estimation stages. Third, it evaluates their standard error
accuracy in a simulation study comparing JS and JSA with MIIV and ML.

The remainder of the article introduces the model and notation, describes the
estimation of factor loadings, latent regression slopes, and the remaining
parameters, presents the analytical standard errors, and reports the
simulation study.

# Model, Notation, and Parameterization

Following the all-y LISREL notation [@joreskog_sorbom_1996, submodel 3B,
Chapter 6; @rosseel_vidal_2025], let $\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^p$ contain the
continuous observed variables and $\boldsymbol\eta\in\mathbb R^q$ the latent
variables. The measurement and latent variable models are

$$
\mathbf y
=
\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\eta
+\boldsymbol\epsilon,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\eta
=
\boldsymbol\alpha+\mathbf B\boldsymbol\eta
+\boldsymbol\zeta,
$$
where $\boldsymbol\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ contains the measurement intercepts,
$\boldsymbol\Lambda\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ contains the factor loadings,
$\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathbb R^q$ contains the structural intercepts, and
$\mathbf B\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$ contains the latent regression slopes,
that is, the regression slopes among the latent variables. The measurement
errors $\boldsymbol\epsilon\in\mathbb R^p$ and structural disturbances
$\boldsymbol\zeta\in\mathbb R^q$ satisfy
$E(\boldsymbol\epsilon)=\mathbf0$ and $E(\boldsymbol\zeta)=\mathbf0$.
Let $\mathbb S_+^k$ and $\mathbb S_{++}^k$ denote the sets of symmetric
positive semidefinite and positive definite $k\times k$ matrices,
respectively. Assume

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\epsilon)
=
\boldsymbol\Theta\in\mathbb S_+^p,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\zeta)
=
\boldsymbol\Psi\in\mathbb S_+^q,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\epsilon,\boldsymbol\zeta)
=
\mathbf0_{p\times q}.
$$

Provided that $\mathbf I_q-\mathbf B$ is nonsingular, the latent and
observed mean vectors are

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_\eta
=
(\mathbf I_q-\mathbf B)^{-1}\boldsymbol\alpha
\in\mathbb R^q,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\mu_y
=
\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\mu_\eta
\in\mathbb R^p,
$$
where $\mathbf I_q$ is the $q\times q$ identity matrix. The implied
observed covariance matrix is

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma
=
\boldsymbol\Lambda(\mathbf I_q-\mathbf B)^{-1}
\boldsymbol\Psi
(\mathbf I_q-\mathbf B)^{-\top}
\boldsymbol\Lambda^\top
+
\boldsymbol\Theta.
$$

Let $\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ collect the free parameters. Assume that $\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$. Denote
the sample mean vector and covariance matrix by
$\overline{\mathbf y}\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\mathbf S\in\mathbb S_+^p$,
respectively, computed from a single group of independent and identically
distributed observations $\mathbf y_i$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, of $\mathbf y$,
which is the setting of all estimation expressions below.^[Following
lavaan, $\mathbf S$ uses the divisor $n$ for JS and JSA and $n-1$ for MIIV
estimation.] Define

$$
\mathbf s
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline{\mathbf y}\\
\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf S)
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^h,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol\mu_y(\boldsymbol\theta)\\
\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)\}
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^h,
\qquad
h=p+\frac{p(p+1)}2,
$$
where $\operatorname{vech}$ stacks the lower triangular entries, including
the diagonal.

# Estimation of Factor Loadings and Latent Regression Slopes

JS, JSA, and MIIV estimate factor loadings and latent regression slopes
equation by equation, under a scaling indicator parameterization
[@bollen_1996; @bollen_2018; @burghgraeve_etall_2021], in which one loading
per latent variable, that of its scaling indicator, is fixed to one and the
corresponding intercept is fixed to zero [@bollen_1989]. These estimates are obtained from centered observations,
with intercepts estimated subsequently. The following example
illustrates how JS and MIIV address measurement error in an observed
predictor.

\begin{lsamexample}\label{ex:loading}
Consider four indicators of $\eta_1$, with $y_1$ as its scaling indicator:
$$
y_1=\eta_1+\epsilon_1,
\qquad
y_r=\nu_r+\lambda_r\eta_1+\epsilon_r,
\quad r=2,3,4.
$$
Assume
$$
E(\epsilon_r)=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_1,\epsilon_r)=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon_r,\epsilon_s)=0
\quad(r\ne s).
$$
The objective is to estimate $\lambda_2$. Writing
$\psi=\operatorname{Var}(\eta_1)$ and
$\omega_1=\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_1)$, the population slope from
regressing $y_2$ directly on $y_1$ is
$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_2)}
     {\operatorname{Var}(y_1)}
=
\lambda_2\frac{\psi}{\psi+\omega_1}.
$$
Thus, measurement error in $y_1$ attenuates the slope.

JS estimates the latent predictor from its scaling indicator. Under joint
normality,
$$
E(\eta_1\mid y_1)
=
\mu_1+R(y_1-\mu_1),
\qquad
R=\frac{\psi}{\psi+\omega_1},
$$
where $\mu_1=E(\eta_1)=E(y_1)$. The other indicators provide information
about $\omega_1$, because
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_3)=\lambda_3\psi,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_4)=\lambda_4\psi,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_4)=\lambda_3\lambda_4\psi.
$$
Consequently,
$$
\psi
=
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_3)\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_4)}
     {\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_4)},
\qquad
\widehat\omega_1
=
s_{11}-\frac{s_{13}s_{14}}{s_{34}},
$$
where $s_{rs}$ denotes a sample covariance. This illustrates the
preliminary error variance calculation using one pair of additional
indicators.

With the small sample correction used in JS, the estimated reliability
adjustment and fitted latent predictor are
$$
\widehat R
=
\frac{s_{11}-c_n\widehat\omega_1}{s_{11}},
\qquad
c_n=\frac{n-3}{n-1},
\qquad
\widetilde\eta_1
=
\overline y_1+\widehat R(y_1-\overline y_1).
$$
Regressing $y_2$ on $\widetilde\eta_1$, with an intercept, gives
$$
\widehat\lambda_{2,\mathrm{JS}}
=
\frac{\widehat R\,s_{12}}{\widehat R^2s_{11}}
=
\frac{s_{12}}{s_{11}-c_n\widehat\omega_1}.
$$

MIIV instead substitutes $\eta_1=y_1-\epsilon_1$ into the equation for
$y_2$:
$$
y_2=\nu_2+\lambda_2y_1+u,
\qquad
u=\epsilon_2-\lambda_2\epsilon_1.
$$
The explanatory variable $y_1$ correlates with the composite error,
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,u)=-\lambda_2\omega_1,
$$
whereas $y_3$ satisfies $\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,u)=0$. It can therefore
serve as an instrument when $\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_1)\ne0$, giving
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_2)
=
\lambda_2\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_1),
\qquad
\widehat\lambda_{2,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\frac{s_{32}}{s_{31}}.
$$
With several instruments, such as $y_3$ and $y_4$, two-stage least squares
first regresses $y_1$ on the instruments and then regresses $y_2$ on the
fitted values, including intercepts in both regressions.

For either estimator,
$$
\widehat\nu_2
=
\overline y_2-\widehat\lambda_2\overline y_1.
$$
JS therefore adjusts the predictor using an estimated measurement error
variance, whereas MIIV uses instruments to estimate the loading despite the
correlation between the explanatory variable and the composite error. JSA
follows the JS calculation using a normalized aggregate of eligible
indicators in place of $y_1$.
\end{lsamexample}

## James–Stein Estimation

Consider one measurement or latent variable equation. Let
$\mathbf f\in\mathbb R^k$ collect its latent predictors and
$\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^k$ the corresponding factor loadings or latent
regression slopes. Let $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^k$ contain their scaling
indicators in the same order, and let $\mathbf e\in\mathbb R^k$ contain the
corresponding measurement errors. The scaling indicator rows of the
measurement model give

$$
\mathbf x=\mathbf f+\mathbf e,
$$
which generalizes $y_1=\eta_1+\epsilon_1$ in the example. Write

$$
\boldsymbol\mu
=
E(\mathbf f)=E(\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^k,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Sigma_x
=
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf x)\in\mathbb S_{++}^k,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Omega
=
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf e)\in\mathbb S_+^k.
$$

The observed dependent variable is the indicator being modeled in a
measurement equation, such as $y_2$ in the example. For a latent variable
equation, the dependent latent variable is replaced by its scaling
indicator. Its error then contains both the structural disturbance and that
scaling indicator's measurement error. Denote the resulting equation error
by $\varepsilon$.

The JS procedures considered use proxies that load only on their respective
latent predictors and have mutually uncorrelated measurement errors, so
$\boldsymbol\Omega$ is diagonal. The required orthogonality conditions are

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf f,\mathbf e)=\mathbf0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf f,\varepsilon)=\mathbf0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf e,\varepsilon)=\mathbf0.
$$

Under joint normality,

$$
E(\mathbf f\mid\mathbf x)
=
\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf R(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu),
\qquad
\mathbf R
=
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_x-\boldsymbol\Omega)
\boldsymbol\Sigma_x^{-1}
\in\mathbb R^{k\times k}.
$$

Without normality, this expression is the best linear predictor of
$\mathbf f$ from $\mathbf x$. JS estimates this predictor and then applies
least squares [@burghgraeve_etall_2021].

Let $\mathbf S_x\in\mathbb S_{++}^k$ contain the sample covariances of the
proxies and $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega}\in\mathbb R^{k\times k}$ be the
diagonal matrix of preliminary measurement error variance estimates. The
estimated reliability adjustment and fitted latent predictors are

$$
\widehat{\mathbf R}
=
(\mathbf S_x-c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega})\mathbf S_x^{-1},
\qquad
c_n=\frac{n-3}{n-1},
$$

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf f}
=
\overline{\mathbf x}
+
\widehat{\mathbf R}(\mathbf x-\overline{\mathbf x}).
$$

Let $\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ contain the centered proxy
observations and $\mathbf d\in\mathbb R^n$ the centered observations of the
dependent variable. The centered fitted predictor matrix is

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf X}
=
\mathbf X\widehat{\mathbf R}^{\top}.
$$

The estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf a}
=
(\widetilde{\mathbf X}^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf X})^{-1}
\widetilde{\mathbf X}^{\top}\mathbf d
=
(\mathbf S_x-c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega})^{-1}
\mathbf s_{xd},
$$
where $\mathbf s_{xd}\in\mathbb R^k$ contains the sample covariances
between the proxies and the dependent variable. The second expression shows
that the fitted predictor regression is equivalent to subtracting the
estimated measurement error contribution from the proxy covariance matrix.
These expressions assume that $\widetilde{\mathbf X}$ has full column rank
and that the loadings and slopes are not subject to equality constraints.

### Scaling James–Stein Estimation

For scaling JS, $\mathbf x$ contains the scaling indicators of the latent
predictors. Preliminary measurement error variances are obtained from the
covariance relationships illustrated in the example. For an indicator
$y_r$, two other eligible indicators $y_s$ and $y_t$ of the same latent
variable give

$$
\widehat\omega_r
=
s_{rr}-\frac{s_{rs}s_{rt}}{s_{st}}.
$$

When several eligible pairs are available, the corresponding estimates are
averaged. The preliminary estimates for the scaling indicators form
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega}$, yielding

$$
\widehat{\mathbf a}_{\mathrm{JS}}
=
(\mathbf S_x-c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega})^{-1}
\mathbf s_{xd}.
$$

These preliminary error variance estimates are used for prediction and need
not equal the final model estimates.

### Aggregated James–Stein Estimation

JSA replaces each scaling indicator by a reliability weighted aggregate of
indicators of the same latent predictor [@burghgraeve_etall_2021]. The
indicators must satisfy the proxy conditions above, which exclude the
dependent indicator when estimating a measurement equation.

For each latent predictor $f$ in $\mathbf f$, let $\mathbf y_f\in\mathbb R^r$
collect its eligible indicators, with corresponding intercepts
$\boldsymbol\nu_f\in\mathbb R^r$ and loadings
$\boldsymbol\lambda_f\in\mathbb R^r$. For weights $\mathbf w\in\mathbb R^r$,
normalizing the aggregate to the latent variable's scale gives

$$
g
=
\frac{\mathbf w^\top(\mathbf y_f-\boldsymbol\nu_f)}
     {\mathbf w^\top\boldsymbol\lambda_f}
=
f+e_g,
$$
where $e_g$ is the aggregate's measurement error. Let
$\mathbf Q_f\in\mathbb S_+^r$ be the diagonal covariance matrix of the
selected indicators' measurement errors. Then

$$
\omega_g
=
\operatorname{Var}(e_g)
=
\frac{\mathbf w^\top\mathbf Q_f\mathbf w}
     {(\mathbf w^\top\boldsymbol\lambda_f)^2}.
$$

Let $\widehat{\mathbf Q}_f$ contain preliminary measurement error variance
estimates and $\mathbf S_f\in\mathbb S_{++}^r$ the sample covariance matrix
of these indicators. The weights maximize estimated reliability:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf w}
\in
\underset{\mathbf w\ne\mathbf0}{\arg\max}
\left(
1-
\frac{\mathbf w^\top\widehat{\mathbf Q}_f\mathbf w}
     {\mathbf w^\top\mathbf S_f\mathbf w}
\right).
$$

Using preliminary scaling JS loadings $\widehat{\boldsymbol\lambda}_f$, the
centered aggregate and its estimated error variance are

$$
\widehat g
=
\frac{\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}
      (\mathbf y_f-\overline{\mathbf y}_f)}
     {\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol\lambda}_f},
\qquad
\widehat\omega_g
=
\frac{\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}
      \widehat{\mathbf Q}_f\widehat{\mathbf w}}
     {(\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol\lambda}_f)^2},
$$
with nonzero normalization denominator.

Constructing one aggregate for each latent predictor gives the columns of
$\mathbf X$, and their estimated error variances form the diagonal of
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega}$, in the same order. The aggregate covariance
matrix and its covariances with the dependent variable replace
$\mathbf S_x$ and $\mathbf s_{xd}$ in the preceding expressions, giving

$$
\widehat{\mathbf a}_{\mathrm{JSA}}
=
(\mathbf S_x-c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega})^{-1}
\mathbf s_{xd}.
$$

Thus, JS and JSA share the estimation formula and differ in the
construction of the proxies and their measurement error variances.

## Model-Implied Instrumental-Variable Estimation

MIIV uses the scaling indicator equations to replace latent variables with
observed variables [@bollen_1996]. For the same equation considered above,
substituting

$$
\mathbf f=\mathbf x-\mathbf e
$$
produces an equation with the scaling indicators as explanatory variables
and composite error

$$
u=\varepsilon-\mathbf a^\top\mathbf e.
$$

The explanatory variables generally correlate with the composite error
because both contain the scaling indicator measurement errors.

After centering and stacking observations, the transformed equation is

$$
\mathbf d=\mathbf X\mathbf a+\mathbf u,
$$
where $\mathbf d\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$
contain the centered dependent observations and scaling indicator
observations defined above, and $\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^n$ contains the
centered composite errors.

The hypothesized model identifies observed instruments
$\mathbf z\in\mathbb R^\ell$ satisfying

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf z,u)=\mathbf0,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}\{\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf z,\mathbf x)\}=k,
\qquad
\ell\geq k.
$$

The first condition concerns instrument validity and the second instrument
relevance.

Let $\mathbf Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times\ell}$ contain the centered instrument
observations. The first stage regresses the explanatory variables on the
instruments:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf X}
=
\mathbf P\mathbf X,
\qquad
\mathbf P
=
\mathbf Z(\mathbf Z^\top\mathbf Z)^{-1}\mathbf Z^\top
\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}.
$$

The second stage regresses the dependent variable on these fitted values:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf a}_{\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
(\widehat{\mathbf X}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf X})^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf X}^{\top}\mathbf d
=
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf P\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf P\mathbf d.
$$

The matrices to be inverted are assumed nonsingular, and the loadings and
slopes are not subject to equality constraints.

Both approaches therefore use fitted predictors in a least squares
regression. JS and JSA construct them through an estimated reliability
adjustment, whereas MIIV constructs them by projecting the scaling
indicators onto model-implied instruments.

# Estimation of Variance, Covariance, and Intercept Parameters

After estimating the factor loadings and latent regression slopes, the
remaining variance and covariance parameters can be estimated using several
least squares procedures [@maydeuolivares_etall_2026]. For all three
estimators, we use reweighted least squares, the default in the
implementations considered, holding the estimated loadings and slopes fixed
throughout the iterations. Let

$$
\widehat{\mathbf H}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Lambda}
(\mathbf I_q-\widehat{\mathbf B})^{-1}
\in\mathbb R^{p\times q},
$$
where $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Lambda}$ and $\widehat{\mathbf B}$ are obtained
using JS, JSA, or MIIV, assuming that $\mathbf I_q-\widehat{\mathbf B}$ is
nonsingular. Conditional on these estimates, the implied covariance matrix
is

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma(\mathbf v)
=
\widehat{\mathbf H}\boldsymbol\Psi(\mathbf v)
\widehat{\mathbf H}^{\top}
+
\boldsymbol\Theta(\mathbf v),
$$
where $\mathbf v\in\mathbb R^{d_v}$ collects the free variance and
covariance parameters.

Conditional on the estimated loadings and slopes, the implied covariance
moments are linear in these parameters [@ernst_etall_2023]. Incorporating
fixed entries and linear equality restrictions gives

$$
\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol\Sigma(\mathbf v)\}
=
\widehat{\mathbf c}+\widehat{\mathbf G}\mathbf v,
$$
where $t=p(p+1)/2$, $\widehat{\mathbf c}\in\mathbb R^t$ is the fixed
component under the chosen parameterization, and
$\widehat{\mathbf G}\in\mathbb R^{t\times d_v}$ maps the free parameters to
the implied covariance moments.

For a weight matrix $\widehat{\mathbf W}\in\mathbb S_{++}^t$, the weighted
least squares estimate is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf v}
=
\left(
\widehat{\mathbf G}^{\top}
\widehat{\mathbf W}
\widehat{\mathbf G}
\right)^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf G}^{\top}
\widehat{\mathbf W}
\left\{
\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf S)-\widehat{\mathbf c}
\right\},
$$
assuming that $\widehat{\mathbf G}$ has full column rank.

Reweighted least squares updates the normal theory weight matrix using the
current implied covariance matrix [@browne_1974; @lee_jennrich_1979]:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf W}^{(\tau)}
=
\frac12\mathbf D_p^\top
\left[
\{\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{(\tau)}\}^{-1}
\otimes
\{\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{(\tau)}\}^{-1}
\right]\mathbf D_p,
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{(\tau)}
=
\boldsymbol\Sigma(\widehat{\mathbf v}^{(\tau)}).
$$

Here, $\otimes$ denotes the Kronecker product, and
$\mathbf D_p\in\mathbb R^{p^2\times t}$ is the duplication matrix
satisfying

$$
\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf S)
=
\mathbf D_p\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf S).
$$

At iteration $\tau$, substituting $\widehat{\mathbf W}^{(\tau)}$ into the
weighted least squares expression gives $\widehat{\mathbf v}^{(\tau+1)}$.
This procedure is repeated until convergence, assuming that the implied
covariance matrices used to construct the weights remain positive definite.
The resulting $\widehat{\mathbf v}$ determines $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Theta}$
and $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Psi}$, which are not constrained to be positive
semidefinite.

Finally, the intercepts are estimated from the sample means, using the
previously estimated factor loadings and latent regression slopes. Under
the scaling indicator parameterization, the mean structure is saturated
when all nonscaling indicator intercepts and all structural intercepts are
free. Let $\overline{\mathbf m}\in\mathbb R^q$ contain the sample scaling
indicator means, ordered by latent variable. Then

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_\eta
=
\overline{\mathbf m},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol\nu}
=
\overline{\mathbf y}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Lambda}\overline{\mathbf m}
\in\mathbb R^p,
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol\alpha}
=
(\mathbf I_q-\widehat{\mathbf B})
\overline{\mathbf m}
\in\mathbb R^q.
$$

These expressions preserve the fixed zero scaling indicator intercepts and
reproduce the observed sample means. Additional mean structure restrictions
require a corresponding constrained estimation step.

Together, these stages estimate the free entries of $\boldsymbol\Lambda$,
$\mathbf B$, $\boldsymbol\Theta$, $\boldsymbol\Psi$, $\boldsymbol\nu$, and
$\boldsymbol\alpha$. Although the estimated factor loadings and latent
regression slopes are held fixed during covariance estimation, their
sampling uncertainty is propagated when calculating standard errors.

# Analytical Standard Errors

## James–Stein Estimation

@burghgraeve_etall_2021 derived a variance expression for the latent
regression slopes that accounts for the estimated reliability adjustment
and used bootstrap standard errors in their evaluations. Here, analytical
standard errors are obtained by differentiating the complete estimation
procedure with respect to the sample moments. For
$T\in\{\mathrm{JS},\mathrm{JSA}\}$, write

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_T
=
g_{n,T}(\mathbf s),
$$
where $g_{n,T}$ maps the $h$ sample moments to the $d$ parameter estimates.
This mapping includes the preliminary error variance estimates, the
estimates of the factor loadings and latent regression slopes, the
subsequent variance and covariance estimates, and the intercept estimates.

Suppose

$$
\sqrt n\{
\mathbf s-\boldsymbol\sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)
\}
\xrightarrow{d}
N_h(\mathbf0,\boldsymbol\Gamma),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Gamma\in\mathbb S_+^h,
$$
where $\boldsymbol\Gamma$ is the joint asymptotic covariance matrix of the
sample means and covariances. Under the required moment and
differentiability conditions, the delta method covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf V}_T
=
\frac1n
\widehat{\mathbf J}_T
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}
\widehat{\mathbf J}_T^\top
\in\mathbb S_+^d,
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf J}_T
=
\left.
\frac{\partial g_{n,T}(\mathbf s)}
     {\partial\mathbf s^\top}
\right|_{\mathbf s=\mathbf s_{\mathrm{obs}}}
\in\mathbb R^{d\times h}.
$$

The Jacobian propagates uncertainty through all estimation stages,
including the intercept estimates. It is evaluated analytically by default,
including implicit differentiation of the converged reweighted least squares
equations. For JSA, it also incorporates derivatives of the estimated
aggregation weights and normalization loadings.

The matrix $\boldsymbol\Gamma$ can be estimated using normal theory or
empirical moments through order four [@browne_1984]. Normal theory
estimates may be evaluated at the sample covariance matrix or the fitted
model covariance matrix. For parameter $r=1,\ldots,d$, the analytical
standard error is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\theta_{T,r})
=
\sqrt{[\widehat{\mathbf V}_T]_{rr}}
\in[0,\infty).
$$

## Model-Implied Instrumental-Variable Estimation

For the MIIV estimates of the factor loadings and latent regression slopes
in one equation, the conventional homoskedastic covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathbf a,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\widehat\sigma_u^{\,2}
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf P\mathbf X)^{-1}
\in\mathbb S_+^k,
$$
where

$$
\widehat\sigma_u^{\,2}
=
\frac{\widehat{\mathbf u}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf u}}
     {n-k-1},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf u}
=
\mathbf d-\mathbf X\widehat{\mathbf a}_{\mathrm{MIIV}}.
$$

The intercept is absorbed by centering, and $n>k+1$ is assumed. Here,
$\sigma_u^2$ is the variance of the composite error in the transformed
equation, rather than an individual measurement error or structural
disturbance variance. This is the default covariance estimator for the MIIV
loadings and slopes in the implementation considered.

For the variance and covariance parameters $\mathbf v$, the delta method
accounts for uncertainty in the previously estimated loadings and slopes
[@bollen_maydeuolivares_2007; @jin_etall_2021]. Define

$$
\widehat{\mathbf H}_2
=
(\widehat{\mathbf G}^{\top}
 \widehat{\mathbf W}
 \widehat{\mathbf G})^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf G}^{\top}
\widehat{\mathbf W}
\in\mathbb R^{d_v\times t},
$$
evaluated at the converged weights and treated as fixed in the
linearization. Let $d_a$ denote the total number of free factor loadings
and latent regression slopes. Let
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_1\in\mathbb R^{t\times d_a}$ be the Jacobian
of the implied covariance moments with respect to these parameters,
evaluated at the estimates, and let
$\widehat{\mathbf K}\in\mathbb R^{d_a\times t}$ be the Jacobian of their
MIIV estimates with respect to $\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf S)$
[@fisher_bollen_2020].

Under correct specification, the covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathbf v,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\frac1n
\widehat{\mathbf H}_2
(\mathbf I_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_1\widehat{\mathbf K})
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}_S
(\mathbf I_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_1\widehat{\mathbf K})^\top
\widehat{\mathbf H}_2^\top
\in\mathbb S_+^{d_v},
$$
where $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}_S\in\mathbb S_+^t$ estimates the
asymptotic covariance matrix of the sample covariance moments. It is the
covariance-moment block of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}$. The factor

$$
\mathbf I_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_1\widehat{\mathbf K}
$$
propagates the sampling uncertainty of the estimated factor loadings and
latent regression slopes through the residual covariance moments.

Moment based covariance estimates are also available for the MIIV factor
loadings and latent regression slopes as

$$
\frac1n
\widehat{\mathbf K}
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}_S
\widehat{\mathbf K}^{\top}.
$$

For the intercepts, moment based standard errors follow by differentiating
the mean structure expressions with respect to the sample moments. These
calculations provide delta method standard errors separately for each
parameter block. In particular, the second stage expression uses the
converged weights as fixed in its linearization, whereas the JS and JSA
Jacobians differentiate the complete estimation procedure. A related delta
method calculation for instrumental variable regression is presented by
@maydeuolivares_etall_2019.

# Simulation Design and Performance Evaluation

In this section we describe the design of the simulation study and the
measures used to evaluate the standard errors.

### Population Model and Estimands

We study the model in @fig-model, with three latent variables and four
indicators each. The latent variable model is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{2}&=\alpha_2+B_{21}\eta_{1}+\zeta_{2},\\
\eta_{3}&=\alpha_3+B_{31}\eta_{1}+B_{32}\eta_{2}+\zeta_{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pop-structural}

The design is partly based on previous studies. @burghgraeve_etall_2021
used four indicators per latent variable, a common reliability of .6 or .8
for all indicators. Note also that the model is similar to the empirical 
illustration in @burghgraeve_etall_2021. Moreover, 
@jin_etall_2021 used a recursive latent variable model with several equations 
and standardized slopes between 0.1 and 0.6, 
which the present model follows partly with $B_{21}=0.6$, $B_{31}=0.3$, and
$B_{32}=0.5$. With $\operatorname{Var}(\eta_1)=1$,
$\operatorname{Var}(\zeta_2)=0.64$, and $\operatorname{Var}(\zeta_3)=0.48$,
the variances of $\eta_2$ and $\eta_3$ equal 1, so that the slopes
are standardized, and the implied correlations are .60 between $\eta_1$
and $\eta_2$, .60 between $\eta_1$ and $\eta_3$, and .68 between $\eta_2$
and $\eta_3$. The scaling indicators have loadings fixed to one and the
remaining loadings range from 0.8 to 1.2. The mean structure has
$E(\eta_1)=1$, $\alpha_2=\alpha_3=0.5$, and intercepts of 0.2 for the
nonscaling indicators. The main estimands are all free factor
loadings, latent regression slopes, residual variances, and latent variances
and disturbance variances.

### Simulation Conditions and Estimation Approaches

We employed a fully factorial design with two factors: sample size
($n\in\{100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600\}$) and indicator reliability
($\rho\in\{.6, .8\}$). This yielded $6\times2=12$ conditions, each
replicated 1,500 times. The sample sizes cover the small to moderate range
in which the equation by equation estimators are expected to differ most
from ML. The reliability levels match the low and high
conditions of @burghgraeve_etall_2021 and determine the size of the
reliability adjustment in JS and JSA. As highlighted throughout the article, 
we investigated the JS, JSA, MIIV, and ML approaches, all
with the default options in lavaan [@rosseel_2012]. 

### Data Generation

Data were generated from the population model with all stochastic
components normal and mutually independent. The exogenous latent variable
was generated as $\eta_1\sim\mathcal{N}(1,1)$ and the structural
disturbances as $\zeta_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.64)$ and
$\zeta_3\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.48)$, from which $\eta_2$ and $\eta_3$ follow
by @eq-pop-structural. The measurement error of each indicator was
generated as normal with mean zero and variance $\lambda^2(1-\rho)/\rho$,
where $\lambda$ is the loading of that indicator, so that every indicator
has reliability $\rho$ in its condition, and the indicators follow by the
measurement equations. The observed variables are therefore multivariate
normal with the mean vector and covariance matrix implied by the
population values. 

### Convergence, Outliers, and Inadmissible Solutions

Replications were screened in two steps, and a replication that failed
either step for any estimator was removed for all four. A solution was
nonconverged when any estimate, standard error, or confidence interval
bound of an estimand was missing or non-finite. Among the converged
replications, outliers were point estimates more than three interquartile
ranges below the first or above the third quartile, per condition,
estimator, and estimand. Inadmissible
solutions, with a nonpositive variance estimate, were retained and
counted.

### Performance Measures

Performance was assessed with the measures implemented in the simhelpers
package [@joshi_pustejovsky_2025], computed for every estimand. These
measures, with their empirical and Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE)
calculations, are listed in @tbl-performance. The MCSEs of the SD and
of the SE$^2$/VAR ratio are obtained by jackknife and that of coverage in
closed form. The SE/SD ratio and the SE$^2$/VAR ratio compare the same
quantities on the standard deviation and on the variance scale, so only
the latter, for which an MCSE is available, is shown in the figures.
Coverage between .925 and .975 and SE$^2$/VAR ratios between 0.90 and 1.10
were considered acceptable.

Although the evaluation targets the standard errors, the relative bias of
the estimates was also computed, because standard errors of markedly
biased estimates are of limited use for inference. It is reported in the
text, but not in the figures.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Performance Measures for Evaluating the Standard Errors"
#| apa-note: "$\\hat\\theta_k$ is the estimate of parameter $\\theta$ in replication $k$ ($k = 1, \\dots, K$) and $\\bar{\\theta}$ the mean of the $K$ estimates. $\\widehat{SE}_k$ is the estimated standard error in replication $k$, $\\overline{SE} = \\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_k \\widehat{SE}_k$, $\\overline{SE^2} = \\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_k \\widehat{SE}_k^2$, and $L_k, U_k$ are the confidence interval limits. The subscript $(j)$ marks a leave-one-out jackknife replicate. The dash marks an MCSE that is not computed."
tab <- data.frame(
  measure = c("Relative bias", "SD", "SE/SD ratio", "SE$^2$/VAR ratio", "Coverage"),
  empirical = c("$(\\bar{\\theta}-\\theta)/\\theta$",
                "$S_{\\hat\\theta}=\\sqrt{\\tfrac{1}{K-1}\\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\\hat\\theta_k-\\bar{\\theta})^2}$",
                "$\\overline{SE}/S_{\\hat\\theta}$",
                "$\\nu=\\overline{SE^2}/S_{\\hat\\theta}^2$",
                "$c=\\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_{k=1}^{K}I(L_k\\le\\theta\\le U_k)$"),
  mcse = c("$S_{\\hat\\theta}/(\\sqrt{K}\\,|\\theta|)$",
           "$\\sqrt{\\tfrac{K-1}{K}\\sum_{j=1}^{K}(S_{(j)}-S_{\\hat\\theta})^2}$",
           "---",
           "$\\sqrt{\\tfrac{K-1}{K}\\sum_{j=1}^{K}(\\nu_{(j)}-\\nu)^2}$",
           "$\\sqrt{c(1-c)/K}$"))
knitr::asis_output(paste0("\\begin{center}\n",
  knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, longtable = TRUE,
               linesep = "", format = "latex",
               col.names = c("Performance measure", "Empirical calculation", "MCSE")),
  "\n\\end{center}"))
```

### Reproducibility and Computational Details

All analyses were conducted in R [@rcoreteam_2026] using the lavaan package
[@rosseel_2012] for estimation, simhelpers [@joshi_pustejovsky_2025] for
performance evaluation, and ggplot2 [@wickham_2016] for the figures. The
computational environment was pinned with Nix [@dolstra_etall_2004] via the
rix package [@rodrigues_baumann_2026], and a Dockerfile that builds the same
environment inside a container is also provided. The article was written
with the apaquarto extension [@schneider_2026]. For an extensive description of all
files and how to reproduce the simulation study as well as the manuscript,
see the repository.

```{r}
#| label: performance
source("performance_calculation.R")
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x)
rb_other <- max(abs(summ$rel_bias[summ$estimator != "IV"]))
rb_iv100 <- summ[summ$estimator == "IV" & summ$n == 100 & summ$rel == 0.6, ]
rb_iv_load <- range(-rb_iv100$rel_bias[grepl("=~", rb_iv100$parameter)])
rb_iv_var <- range(rb_iv100$rel_bias[grepl("^eta[0-9]~~", rb_iv100$parameter)])
rb_300 <- max(abs(summ$rel_bias[summ$n >= 300]))
summ$estimator <- factor(summ$estimator, levels = c("JS", "JSA", "IV", "ML"))

## long format over the three criteria, with MCSE bars
crit <- c(sd = "SD", rb_var = "SE²/VAR", coverage = "Coverage")
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(crit), function(k)
  data.frame(summ[c("n", "rel", "estimator", "parameter")],
             criterion = crit[k], value = summ[[k]],
             mcse = summ[[paste0(k, "_mcse")]])))
long$criterion <- factor(long$criterion, levels = crit)
long$rel <- factor(long$rel, levels = rels,
                   labels = paste("Reliability", sub("^0", "", rels)))
long$lower <- long$value - long$mcse
long$upper <- long$value + long$mcse

## SE²/VAR values above `cap` are drawn at `cap` with an open triangle and no bar
cap <- 1.5
i <- long$criterion == "SE²/VAR"
long$clipped <- i & long$value > cap
long$value[long$clipped] <- cap
long$upper[i] <- pmin(long$upper[i], cap)
long$lower[long$clipped] <- long$upper[long$clipped] <- NA

ref <- data.frame(criterion = factor(c("SE²/VAR", "Coverage"), levels = crit),
                  y = c(1, 0.95))
pd <- position_dodge(width = 25)

plot_params <- function(pars, labels, breaks = ns) {
  v <- long[long$parameter %in% pars, ]
  v$parameter <- factor(v$parameter, levels = pars, labels = labels)
  ggplot(v, aes(n, value, colour = estimator, shape = estimator,
                linetype = estimator)) +
    geom_hline(data = ref, aes(yintercept = y), colour = "grey55",
               linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0,
                  linetype = "solid", position = pd, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, position = pd) +
    geom_point(size = 2, position = pd) +
    geom_point(data = v[v$clipped, ], shape = 2, size = 3, position = pd,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_grid(rel + criterion ~ parameter, scales = "free_y", switch = "y",
               labeller = labeller(parameter = label_parsed)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = breaks) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(JS = "#2a78d6", JSA = "#eda100",
                                   IV = "#eb6834", ML = "#1baf7a")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(JS = 16, JSA = 18, IV = 15, ML = 17)) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(JS = "solid", JSA = "dashed",
                                     IV = "longdash", ML = "dotdash")) +
    labs(x = expression(italic(n)), y = NULL, colour = "Estimator",
         shape = "Estimator", linetype = "Estimator") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 90),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey80"))
}
pars_coef <- c("eta2~eta1", "eta3~eta1", "eta3~eta2")
lab_coef  <- c("B[21]", "B[31]", "B[32]")
pars_load <- c("eta1=~y2", "eta2=~y6", "eta3=~y10")
lab_load  <- c("lambda[2]", "lambda[6]", "lambda[10]")
pars_res  <- c("y1~~y1", "y2~~y2", "y5~~y5", "y6~~y6", "y9~~y9", "y10~~y10")
lab_res   <- c("theta[1]", "theta[2]", "theta[5]", "theta[6]", "theta[9]",
               "theta[10]")
pars_fvar <- c("eta1~~eta1", "eta2~~eta2", "eta3~~eta3")
lab_fvar  <- c("Var(eta[1])", "Var(zeta[2])", "Var(zeta[3])")
```

# Results

## Convergence, Outliers, and Inadmissible Solutions

All four estimators converged in every replication of every condition.
Outlier screening removed `r scr$removed` of the 18,000 replications
(`r sprintf("%.2f", scr$removed_pct)`%), concentrated at $n=100$ with
reliability .6, where `r sprintf("%.1f", scr$removed_by_cond[1])`% of the
replications were removed, flagged mainly through JS
(`r sprintf("%.1f", scr$flagged_100_06["JS"])`% of the replications in that
condition). In every other condition fewer than 0.5% of the replications were
removed. Inadmissible solutions occurred in `r scr$inad` replications, all
for JS at $n=100$ with reliability .6, where a disturbance variance
estimate was negative. All of them were also flagged by the outlier
screening, so none enters the results below.

## Relative Bias

JS, JSA, and ML were essentially unbiased, with absolute relative bias of at
most `r pct(rb_other)`% for any parameter and condition. MIIV was also nearly
unbiased except at reliability .6 and small samples. At $n=100$ its loadings
were slightly underestimated, by `r pct(rb_iv_load[1])` to
`r pct(rb_iv_load[2])`%, whereas its latent and disturbance variances were
overestimated by `r pct(rb_iv_var[1])` to `r pct(rb_iv_var[2])`%. From
$n=300$ onward, all estimators were within `r pct(rb_300)`% of the population
values.

## Standard Error Performance

Each figure presents reliability .6 in the upper half and .8 in the lower
half. @fig-sim-structural shows the latent regression slopes,
@fig-sim-loadings one loading per latent variable, @fig-sim-residual the
residual variances of the scaling indicators and one nonscaling indicator per
latent variable, and @fig-sim-factorvar the variance of $\eta_1$ and the two
disturbance variances. Omitted loadings and residual variances behave similarly 
to those shown for the same latent variable, with SE$^2$/VAR ratios that differ 
by at most 0.15 and coverage by .03 in every condition.

Overall, standard error performance was acceptable. Across all conditions,
estimators, and parameters, `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(summ$coverage >=.925 & summ$coverage <= .975))`% 
of coverage rates fell between .925 and .975
and `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(summ$rb_var >= .90 & summ$rb_var <= 1.10))`%
of SE$^2$/VAR ratios between 0.90 and 1.10, with no ratio below 0.90. From
$n=300$ onward, the few ratios above 1.10 remained below 1.12. Three
departures emerge at $n=100$ and $n=200$, mainly at reliability .6.

First, JS standard errors for $B_{31}$ and $B_{32}$ exceed the acceptable
range at reliability .6, with SE$^2$/VAR ratios of 1.5–1.6 at $n=100$ and
1.13–1.14 at $n=200$. Coverage nonetheless exceeds .975 only for $B_{31}$ at
$n=100$. Its SD is also the largest, 0.24 versus 0.13–0.17 at $n=100$. These
patterns may reflect instability in the reliability adjustment for the
$\eta_3$ equation. In some replications, the implied correlation between
$\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$ approaches 1, making the fitted predictors nearly
collinear and inflating both estimates and standard errors. Screening removed
the most extreme cases, but milder cases remain. JSA, which aggregates
indicators within each latent variable, shows no corresponding instability.

Second, MIIV loading intervals fall below the acceptable coverage range at
reliability .6, with coverage of .88–.90 at $n=100$, compared with .93–.96 for
the other estimators, despite SE$^2$/VAR ratios of 0.98–1.14 and the smallest
SD. This discrepancy reflects the downward loading bias reported above,
consistent with the weak instrument effect described by @jin_etall_2021, and
diminishes slowly as sample size increases.

Third, at $n=100$ MIIV overestimates the standard errors of the latent and
disturbance variances, with ratios of 1.11–1.18, but its coverage rates of
.96–.97 remain within the acceptable range. ML, in contrast, has ratios close
to 1 but coverage rates of .91–.94 for the disturbance variances. JS and JSA
fall between them. At reliability .8, the coverage rate for the disturbance
variance of $\eta_2$ is about .92 for ML, JS, and JSA, just below the
acceptable range. Residual variances show less contrast, with coverage rates
from .91 to .96 across estimators and a common dip at $n=100$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-structural
#| fig-cap: "Performance of the Standard Errors of the Latent Regression Slopes"

plot_params(pars_coef, lab_coef)
```

# Discussion

This article described MIIV, JS, and JSA estimation as currently implemented in 
the R package lavaan. It also developed and illustrated analytical standard 
errors for JS and JSA. A reproducible simulation study evaluated their
standard error accuracy against ML under correct model specification.

The findings broadly align with the studies that motivated the simulation
design. @bollen_2018, summarizing @bollen_etall_2007, reports few differences
between MIIV and ML under correct specification with normally distributed
data. Our results agree in terms of bias and standard error accuracy from
$n=300$ onward, although MIIV remained less precise than ML for the latent
regression slopes. @jin_etall_2021 found that low scaling indicator
reliability can lead to biased MIIV estimates in small samples and that
standard errors for variance parameters were the least accurate. Related
patterns appeared here at reliability .6 and $n=100$, with loading bias and
undercoverage, alongside inflated standard errors for latent and disturbance
variances. @burghgraeve_etall_2021 found JS less efficient than JSA for latent
regression estimation and JSA competitive with ML, consistent with the
empirical standard deviations observed here. However, their bootstrap standard
errors for JS were too small in small samples, whereas our analytical standard
errors were too large at reliability .6 and $n\le200$. Whether this difference
reflects the standard error methods or differences in the simulation
conditions requires further investigation.

The simulation was intended as a focused evaluation rather than an exhaustive
comparison. Further research should compare MIIV, JS, and JSA across a broader
range of conditions, including departures from normality and misspecification
of the measurement and latent variable models.
